transcript.text:
Sorry to hear the hob's playing up. "Not working properly" can mean a few different things, so here are the usual suspects, simplest first: 1. Key or child lock: most touch-control hobs have a lock (a key or padlock symbol) that stops the zones coming on. Usually you hold that symbol for a few seconds to release it. If the zones work once it's off, that was all it was.
2. The pan (induction only): induction needs a flat, magnetic pan big enough to cover the zone. Check a fridge magnet sticks firmly to the base, and try a pan you know works on another zone. If the known-good pan heats, it was the cookware, not the hob.
3. The supply: check the hob's isolator switch (often a large switch on the wall or in a cupboard nearby) is on, and that no breaker has dropped in the fuse box. If a breaker keeps tripping, don't keep resetting it; that needs an engineer.
4. A faulty part: if one zone stays dead after those checks, it's most likely that zone's element or its control switch on a ceramic or solid-plate hob, or its coil or power module on induction. If every zone is dead, it points more to the supply or the hob's main power board. To narrow it down: what type of hob is it (induction, ceramic glass with red glowing rings, solid plates, or gas), and is it one zone playing up or all of them? Also, what is it doing: not heating at all, heating weakly, cutting out, or showing a code?
It's a ceramic one with red rings, a Zanussi. Just the rear right zone isn't heating, the other three are fine. The display shows the power level ok but it doesn't glow or get hot.

That pattern helps a lot. If three zones heat and the display accepts a power level for the fourth, the power supply, the main board and any child lock are probably fine (a lock would normally stop you setting a level at all). 1. The radiant element for that zone has failed. The coil under the glass burns through with age and goes open circuit, so it gets no power and never glows. This is the most common cause by some way.
2. That zone's control has failed. On a knob hob that's the energy regulator behind the knob. On a touch hob it's usually the relay on the control board that switches that zone. The display can still show a level even if the relay never closes.
3. A loose or burnt wire or connector to the element. This is less common, but it does happen, especially on the higher-power rear zones. 1. Tell me if it's knobs or touch controls. That decides whether the control suspect is a regulator or the board.
2. Switch the rear right zone on and listen closely near the glass. On many touch hobs you'll hear a faint click as the relay switches the element in. A click but no glow points to the element or its wiring. No click (when other zones do click) leans towards the control.
3. If it's a dual or extended zone (two rings drawn on the glass), try both settings. If one ring glows and the other doesn't, it's part of the element or its dual switch, not the whole circuit.
4. Look at the glass over that zone in good light. Any crack or chip means stop using the hob and isolate it, as that changes things. To confirm which part has failed, the element or regulator needs a continuity check. That usually means isolating the hob at the switch or breaker and lifting it out of the worktop, which is a job for an engineer unless you're confident doing it. Let me know the control type and what you hear, and we can pin it down.

It's touch controls. I can't really tell if there's a click, I couldn't hear one. Not sure if it's a dual zone. There was a slight burnt smell from that ring once a couple of weeks ago, but not since.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. Most often the element's coil burnt through. Sometimes it's the connection to it scorching. Because a burnt connection can be a fire risk, please don't use the hob until a qualified engineer has checked it. Switch it off at the hob's isolator switch or breaker for now. 1. The rear right radiant element has failed. The display taking a power level and the other three zones working both fit this, and it's the most common cause by far. The smell may have been the element failing, though spilt food burning off can also cause a one-off smell.
2. A burnt wire or terminal at that element. This is more likely than usual here because of the smell, and an engineer will want to inspect it either way. If it's scorched, the wiring or connector is usually replaced along with the element.
3. The relay for that zone on the touch control board. This is less likely. Not hearing a click doesn't tell us much, as those clicks are often too faint to hear over the room. What suggests it is a continuity check on the element and a look at its connections. That means lifting the hob out with the power isolated, so it's one for the engineer. With the hob switched off and cold, you can safely do one thing: look closely at the glass over that zone in good light. Cracks, or dark or brown discolouration around that ring, are worth telling the engineer about. To help the engineer arrive with the right part, it's worth getting the model and product numbers. A replacement element is normally a reasonable repair on a hob that's otherwise working well.
